subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Gambler's Fallacy
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Gambler's Fallacy usable.

hook.text: A roulette wheel lands red five times. Gamblers pile onto black. The odds haven't changed at all.

buildup.text: The gambler's fallacy: believing past random events change the probability of future independent events.

discovery.text: Each spin is independent. The wheel has no memory. Red five times doesn't make black more likely.

twist.text: In 1913 at Monte Carlo, black came up 26 times in a row. Millions were lost betting on red.

climax.text: Our brains expect patterns in randomness. We see streaks as signals—but coins don't keep score.

quiz.question: What is the gambler's fallacy?
options: Believing past random events affect future probabilities

details.summary: The gambler's fallacy is the mistaken belief that past random events affect future ones. After a coin lands heads five times, people expect tails, but each flip is independent with the same 50-50 odds. The universe has no memory of previous outcomes in truly random processes.
details.whyItMatters: The gambler's fallacy affects gambling, investing, and any decision involving probability. Recognizing it prevents costly errors in risk assessment.
takeaways: Past random events do not influence future random events
Each coin flip is independent regardless of previous outcomes
The fallacy extends to investing, hiring, and risk assessment

faq.question: Is there ever a time when past events predict future ones?
faq.answer: Yes, when events are not independent. A hot hand in basketball may reflect genuine changes in confidence or rhythm. A run of machine failures may signal a real mechanical problem. The gambler's fallacy applies specifically to independent random events, not to correlated sequences.

faq.question: How does the gambler's fallacy affect real decisions?
faq.answer: Asylum judges are less likely to grant a claim after granting several in a row. Loan officers reject more after approving several. Baseball umpires call more strikes after calling consecutive balls. In each case, decision-makers mistakenly expect outcomes to balance out in the short run.
